passage: At the school gate in Toronto, Maria watched Simran's aunt lean in with open arms. “Come here, give Aunty a big hug!” Simran's shoulders rose. She took a small step back, then held out her hand. “Hello, Aunty,” she said. The aunt paused, then laughed and shook the hand warmly. Later, when Simran's cousin Ravi ran up, Simran gave him a high-five and a huge grin. Maria noticed she chose differently each time. She wondered whether Simran had felt uneasy with the hug, or was only shy that morning. When Simran waved goodbye to the aunt, the aunt waved back, smiling.

qa.q: What did Simran do when her aunt opened her arms?
qa.a: She stepped back and held out her hand to shake.

qa.q: What might Simran have felt when her aunt offered a hug, and what else could explain her choice?
qa.a: She may have felt uneasy or not in the mood for a hug, though Maria admits she might just have been shy that morning.

qa.q: What made the moment go well for both of them?
qa.a: Simran offered another greeting and her aunt accepted it warmly, so nobody was pushed.

qa.q: How might Simran's aunt have felt when the hug was declined?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised for a moment, and her laugh and warm handshake suggest she accepted it kindly.

grounding: A child chooses handshake, high-five or wave instead of a hug depending on comfort, and the adult accepts it.

passage:
Saturday. At the temple courtyard, Nikita's neighbour asked for a hug. Nikita went stiff and shook her head, then gave a fist bump. The neighbour said, “Okay, that works too.”

Sunday. At her cousin's birthday, Nikita ran to her best friend Tanuja and threw both arms round her. They both squealed.

The following Saturday. The neighbour saw Nikita and said, “Hello, would you like a wave or a fist bump today?” Nikita smiled and gave a wave. She told Tanuja, “It feels good when people ask.”

qa.q: Who did Nikita hug at her cousin's birthday?
qa.a: Her best friend Tanuja.

qa.q: What was Nikita probably feeling when she went stiff and shook her head at the temple?
qa.a: She was probably uncomfortable with the hug, and offering a fist bump gave her a way to greet without one.

qa.q: What did the neighbour do that helped?
qa.a: The neighbour accepted the fist bump and later asked whether Nikita wanted a wave or a fist bump.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's hug feel different to Nikita from the neighbour's request?
qa.a: Nikita chose Tanuja's hug freely and happily, while the neighbour's request came from someone she was less at ease with.

grounding: A child chooses among hug, fist bump and wave depending on comfort and has the right to decline a hug.

subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage: When Irawati joined our class in the middle of term, she stood by the door holding her bag with both hands. I remembered my own first day at a new school and how loud it felt. I smiled and waved, and she waved back very small. At lunch I patted the empty place next to me. “Do you want to sit here?” She nodded and sat. I offered her half of my orange, and she took one piece. I'm not chatty, so I just showed her where the water cooler and library are. She smiled all the way back to class. I'm Sarika, and that is enough for me.

qa.q: Where was Irawati standing when she first came in?
qa.a: By the door, holding her bag with both hands.

qa.q: Why did Sarika smile and wave at Irawati?
qa.a: Sarika remembered how loud a first day at a new school felt, and wanted the newcomer to feel welcome.

qa.q: What can a shy child do to welcome a new classmate?
qa.a: A shy child can wave, offer a seat, share a snack or show the water cooler and library, as Sarika did.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt during the first lunch?
qa.a: Irawati was probably nervous and relieved to be invited, since she nodded, took an orange piece and smiled on the way back.

grounding: A child welcomes a new classmate with a wave, a seat, a snack and a tour, and even a shy child can do it.

subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage: Teacher's note, Class 4. A new boy, Noor, joined today. Hafsa was sitting nearest the door. Before I could say anything, she stood up, said “Welcome, I'm Hafsa,” and pulled out the chair beside her. She showed him the shelf where the pencil box goes and gave him one of her biscuits at break. Noor did not say much, but he stayed close to her all day and copied her folding of the worksheet. Hafsa is usually quiet in class, so I was struck by how easily she took the lead. I will ask her to help him again tomorrow. Mr. Iqbal.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa show Noor the pencil box goes?
qa.a: On the shelf.

qa.q: What did the teacher think about Hafsa's welcome?
qa.a: He was struck that Hafsa, who is usually quiet, took the lead so easily.

qa.q: How could Mr. Iqbal support this welcome further?
qa.a: He could ask Hafsa to help Noor again tomorrow, as he plans, and also let Noor meet other children.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt during the first day?
qa.a: Noor said little but stayed close to Hafsa all day, which suggests feeling unsure and comforted by her company.

grounding: A child says hello, offers a seat, shares a snack and shows the new student around, and the teacher observes.

passage: Under the banyan tree behind the school in a small town in Punjab, Sarita was teaching Himani the rules of kho-kho. “One team sits in a line, all facing different ways. The chaser runs, and when she taps someone's back and says ‘kho,’ they swap.” Himani frowned. “But why can't the chaser turn round?” Sarita paused. “Because then she'd catch everyone easily. It wouldn't be fair.” Himani nodded, then she picked up a stick and drew the line in the dust to show it again. “Like this?” “Yes!” said Sarita, and she felt very pleased that she could explain it.

qa.q: Where was Sarita teaching the rules?
qa.a: Under the banyan tree behind the school.

qa.q: Why did Sarita feel pleased at the end?
qa.a: She was happy that she had explained the game so well that Himani could show it back, drawing the line in the dust.

qa.q: What question from Himani helped the explanation go deeper?
qa.a: Himani asked why the chaser cannot turn round, and answering it made the reason for the rule clear.

qa.q: How might it feel for Himani to be taught by a friend and not a teacher?
qa.a: Himani may feel relaxed asking questions and testing her understanding by drawing, since a friend does not seem to judge.

grounding: A child explains the rules of a game clearly to show understanding, and a why question encourages depth.

passage: At break in a Cape Town classroom, Zanele asked Alejandro what “brave” meant, because a teacher had used it in the story. Alejandro thought. “It means you're scared, but you do the thing anyway.” Zanele squinted. “So if I'm not scared, I'm not brave?” Alejandro scratched his head. “Maybe. Or maybe it's brave to do something hard even if I'm not scared of it.” “That's more like it,” said Zanele. He turned to his notebook and wrote the word and his own short definition under it. Zanele nodded. “Now I can explain it to my little sister.”

qa.q: What word did Zanele ask about?
qa.a: “Brave.”

qa.q: What was Alejandro trying to show when he explained brave, and how do you know he was still thinking?
qa.a: He was showing he understood the word, and he scratched his head and changed his definition after Zanele's question, which shows he was still working it out.

qa.q: How did Zanele's question help?
qa.a: Zanele's question, “So if I'm not scared, I'm not brave?” pushed Alejandro to think more deeply and improve his explanation.

qa.q: Why might Zanele want to explain the word to a little sister?
qa.a: Explaining it to a younger child would help Zanele check the meaning and share it, and it shows Zanele understood it.

grounding: A child defines a word to show understanding, and a why or how question makes the definition deeper.

passage: Counsellor's note. In the reading group, Ankita was asked to tell us about the story we had all read. She started, “First the boy found a lamp, and then there was a shop, and then his mother was worried, and then…” and stopped, tangled. I asked, “What is the one thing that matters most?” She thought and said, “The boy kept the lamp safe.” Then she added, “Sorry, the middle part wasn't clear.” I told her that it is a good habit to say so, and that I too sometimes lose my way. Next time we will list three key points first. Ms. Jyoti.

qa.q: What did Ankita say was not clear?
qa.a: The middle part.

qa.q: What was Ankita probably feeling when she stopped, tangled in her summary?
qa.a: She was likely a bit flustered, and her apology shows she was aware her middle part was muddled.

qa.q: What method does the counsellor plan to use next time?
qa.a: Ms. Jyoti plans to have the group list three key points first, to help choose what matters.

qa.q: How might the other children in the group benefit from hearing this exchange?
qa.a: They see that an adult also loses the way and admits it, so they may feel safer saying when something is unclear.

grounding: A child learns to summarise a story in a few lines and to clarify a muddled point, and adults model admitting when something was not clear.

passage: Friday night diary. Today Miss Parul asked us to tell the class about our library book in only three sentences. I usually talk on and on! I wrote mine: “Ravi finds a lost puppy. He asks everyone in the colony whose it is. In the end he keeps it because nobody comes.” Miss said it was clear. Then I explained the part about the ladder, and Parul said, “I still don't get that,” and I realised I hadn't told it well. I said, “Oh, I'll say it again,” and did. Mummy says it's okay not to be perfect. I'll try three sentences again tomorrow. Vasudha.

qa.q: How many sentences did Miss Parul ask for?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What did Vasudha realise when Parul said she did not get the part about the ladder?
qa.a: Vasudha realised she had not told that part well, so she offered to say it again.

qa.q: What could Vasudha try to do next to improve her summaries?
qa.a: Vasudha could pick the key points first, keep to three sentences and be ready to clarify a muddled part.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt when she asked about the ladder?
qa.a: Parul was probably curious and wanted to follow the story, and asking helped Vasudha see what was unclear.

grounding: A child learns to summarise a story in three sentences and to clarify a muddled point.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 3. During the drawing lesson, Zainab held up her paper and asked, “Is this correct? You said to colour inside the lines, and then use blue for the sky.” She repeated my whole instruction back to me before I could answer. I noticed some pupils smile at this. I told her, “You have followed each step, and your sky is even.” She relaxed. I take this as a child working hard at learning, not as doubt in herself. I will keep giving specific comments like that, not just “good.” Ms. Rehana.

qa.q: What colour did Zainab use for the sky?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What did the teacher take Zainab's question to mean?
qa.a: She saw it as effort to learn and not as a lack of confidence.

qa.q: Why is the teacher's answer helpful?
qa.a: It names what Zainab did right, following each step and colouring the sky evenly, and does not just say good.

qa.q: How might the other pupils who smiled see Zainab's question?
qa.a: They may find it unusual to repeat the instructions, but it is a way to check understanding, and Zainab may not mind.

grounding: A child repeats an instruction back to check understanding, and the adult treats it as effort to learn and answers with specifics.

passage: Tuesday. In maths I asked Miss Aditi, “Should I subtract before I carry? Is that right?” and I said her steps back to her. Some kids looked at me like I was being annoying, but Miss said, “Yes, that's a careful way to check.” Then she told me exactly which step was right and which one to fix. I liked that she didn't just say “good.” Mama says I ask a lot of questions, but I think asking is how I learn. Tomorrow I will do the same again when I don't understand fractions. Zainab.

qa.q: Who did the writer ask about subtraction?
qa.a: Miss Aditi.

qa.q: Why did Zainab repeat the steps back to Miss Aditi?
qa.a: Zainab wanted to check understanding, because asking is how Zainab learns.

qa.q: What made Miss Aditi's reply helpful?
qa.a: She named which step was right and which to fix, rather than just saying good.

qa.q: How might the classmates who looked annoyed be feeling?
qa.a: They may be impatient or curious, but Zainab's careful checking may help them notice what they too are unsure about.

grounding: A child asks did I do it right and repeats instructions to check, and the teacher treats it as learning effort and answers with specifics.

passage: Tushar, you asked me how to help a friend who is quiet. Listen. When I was eleven, my friend Omkar came to school and didn't take out his tiffin. He sat, looking at his hands. I asked, “Are you okay?” He said, “Mm. Fine.” But I stayed near him and didn't push. At the end of the day he said quietly, “My dog is sick.” I said, “I'm sorry.” That was all. If he'd not told me, that would have been all right too. The asking mattered, and the waiting. A friend needs to know you noticed, even if the answer isn't ready yet.

qa.q: How old was the storyteller when Omkar didn't take out his tiffin?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: Why did the storyteller stay near Omkar after he said he was fine?
qa.a: The storyteller sensed something was wrong and wanted him to know someone cared, without pressing him to answer.

qa.q: What can a child do after asking are you okay and hearing fine?
qa.a: Stay nearby, wait and be ready to listen, as the storyteller did.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt when he was asked and then left space?
qa.a: He probably felt cared for and safe enough to share about his dog in his own time.

grounding: A child asks a friend are you okay when noticing quiet behaviour, and the friend may not answer yet.

passage: The lift was stuck and the lights flickered while Gurleen and Nilesh stood inside with two grown-ups. Nilesh was always chatty, but now he was staring at the floor and biting his lip. Gurleen leaned in and whispered, “Are you okay?” Nilesh shook his head slightly. “I don't like small places.” “Want to hold my sleeve?” she said. He took it. She talked softly about her rabbit until the lift jolted and the doors opened. Outside, Nilesh took a big breath. “Thanks for asking,” he said. Gurleen shrugged. “You looked scared.”

qa.q: What did Gurleen talk softly about?
qa.a: Her rabbit.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling in the stuck lift, and what showed it?
qa.a: He was scared of the small space, which showed in his silence, staring at the floor and biting his lip.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that helped in the stuck lift?
qa.a: She asked if he was okay, offered her sleeve and talked calmly about her rabbit.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt when Nilesh thanked her?
qa.a: She may have felt pleased that her question helped, though she shrugged as if it was a small thing. 🙂

grounding: A child asks are you okay when noticing a friend's quiet fear, and the friend answers in the moment.

passage: At the mela near Tanvir's village, a man selling toy drums told Damini that his drum was made in one afternoon by a famous drummer. Damini raised an eyebrow. “I think you're joking,” Tanvir said, quietly, tapping the drum. “It has a factory sticker.” The man laughed and said, “You are sharp, boy. I was joking.” Tanvir wasn't sure. He wondered if the man was cheating or just teasing. Damini pulled his sleeve. “Let's ask at the next stall before we buy.” At the next stall, they learned the price was half. They went back to the first stall and thanked him, then walked on.

qa.q: What sticker did Tanvir notice on the drum?
qa.a: A factory sticker.

qa.q: What made Tanvir doubt the drum seller's story?
qa.a: The story did not add up, since the drum had a factory sticker, though he was not sure whether the man was cheating or teasing.

qa.q: What did the children do that was smart?
qa.a: They checked the price at another stall before buying, treating doubt as a reason to check facts.

qa.q: How might the drum seller feel when a child questions his story?
qa.a: He may feel amused or caught out, and his laugh leaves it unclear whether he was joking or trying to sell.

grounding: A child voices doubt when a story does not add up, and treats suspicion as a cue to check facts, not a verdict on character.

passage: Thabo listened to Lucia tell the class that her cousin had a pet lion in a garden shed. He put his hand up. “I think you're joking, Lucia.” Lucia grinned. “Maybe.” The class laughed. Thabo was not sure. Could she be teasing or could she have misheard? He asked, “Can you show us a photo?” Lucia said, “No, my cousin lives far away. I made up the lion part; the pet is a tortoise.” Thabo nodded. “The tortoise is good, too,” he said. He felt relieved that he had asked and had not just decided she was lying.

qa.q: Where did Lucia say the lion lived?
qa.a: In a garden shed.

qa.q: Why did Thabo ask for a photo instead of deciding Lucia was lying?
qa.a: He was unsure whether Lucia was teasing or had got it wrong, so he asked her for a photo instead of deciding she was lying.

qa.q: What lesson does Thabo's way of asking show?
qa.a: Doubt is a signal to check the facts, and it does not mean the other person is a bad person.

qa.q: How might Lucia have felt when Thabo asked for a photo?
qa.a: Lucia might have felt caught in a fib but not attacked, since Thabo asked kindly and she felt able to explain.

grounding: A child voices doubt about a tall story and asks for a photo, treating suspicion as a cue to check facts.

passage: Jyoti, I'll tell you about the day I learned to say “I'm not sure.” I was ten, in Class 5. Miss Ankita asked us to explain how a seed grows, and I said, “Oh, I get it,” though I didn't. I wrote nonsense on the board and the class laughed. Miss Ankita didn't. She said, “It's brave to say, ‘I'm not sure.’ Then we can look together.” The next time she asked, I said, “I'm not sure about the roots.” She drew a picture, and I finally understood. Since then, I match my words to how much I really know.

qa.q: How old was the speaker in Class 5?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: Why did the speaker say “I get it” when it wasn't true?
qa.a: The speaker wanted to look as if understanding and probably feared being judged for not knowing.

qa.q: What did Miss Ankita do that helped?
qa.a: She called it brave to say “I'm not sure” and offered to look together, then drew a picture.

qa.q: What would change if Miss Ankita had laughed with the class?
qa.a: The speaker might have learned to hide gaps in knowledge and never asked for help again.

grounding: A child who says I get it or I am not sure learns to match confidence to knowledge, and a supportive teacher rewards admitting a gap.

passage: The power cut plunged Class 4 into darkness in the middle of the science lesson, and the only light came from Mr. Anirban's small torch. He asked who could explain how magnets work. Dolma raised her hand, then lowered it. “Sir, I think I understand about poles, but I'm not sure about why they push apart.” The room was noisy with rain outside. Mr. Anirban said, “That is a good thing to say.” He placed two magnets on the desk under the torch and let her try them. Dolma pushed the two same ends together and felt the push. “I get it now,” she said.

qa.q: What was the only light source in the classroom?
qa.a: Mr. Anirban's small torch.

qa.q: Why did Dolma lower her hand and then say she was not sure about part of the answer?
qa.a: She knew part of it but was honest about the gap, matching her confidence to what she really understood.

qa.q: How did Mr. Anirban help her learn?
qa.a: He praised her honesty and let her try the two magnets herself, so she felt the push.

qa.q: How might the rest of the class benefit from hearing Dolma admit a gap?
qa.a: They see that saying you are not sure is acceptable, so they may feel safer asking for help.

grounding: A child says I am not sure about part and I get it after help, and a supportive teacher rewards admitting a gap.

passage: Last week, Karthik and I argued about whether the class plant needed more water. I said yes, he said no. When he showed me the soil was still damp, I felt hot in the face. I said, “Okay, you're right.” It was hard. Then I added, “But it still looks droopy, so maybe we check the sun.” Miss Suvarna smiled. Later Karthik said, “Thanks for listening.” I thought that conceding would feel like losing, but it felt more like working things out together. I'm Asif, and I still like being right, but I like plants growing better.

qa.q: What did Asif and Karthik argue about?
qa.a: Whether the class plant needed more water.

qa.q: How did Asif feel when he saw the damp soil, and how do you know?
qa.a: Asif felt embarrassed or stung about being wrong, since his face went hot and conceding was hard.

qa.q: What did Asif do that turned the argument into teamwork?
qa.a: He conceded with “Okay, you're right” and then added a new idea about checking the sun.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when Asif conceded?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt respected and relieved, since he thanked Asif for listening.

grounding: A child concedes with okay you're right and qualifies with but, and learns conceding is not losing.

passage: Observation note, Class 6. During the debate on school uniform, Sarika argued that uniforms should be worn every day. A classmate, Lavanya, made a strong point about comfort in hot weather. Sarika paused for a moment and said, “Okay, you're right about the heat. But maybe we can keep uniforms and choose lighter cloth?” The room got quiet, then some students nodded. I praised her for saying so gracefully. Afterwards she told me she felt a little sad, as if she'd lost something. I explained that changing her mind is thinking, not losing. She thought about that. Mr. Menon.

qa.q: What was the debate about?
qa.a: School uniform.

qa.q: What did Sarika feel after conceding the point?
qa.a: She felt a little sad, as if she had lost something, though she was open to hearing that changing her mind is not losing.

qa.q: What did Sarika's qualifying sentence add?
qa.a: She kept part of her view and offered a new idea about lighter cloth, so the class could work on a middle way.

qa.q: How might Lavanya have felt when Sarika conceded?
qa.a: Lavanya probably felt heard and pleased that her point about the heat was taken seriously.

grounding: A child concedes a point and qualifies it with but, and an adult praises conceding gracefully and says it is not losing.

passage: Joseph, you asked me how to argue without a fight. Here's a story. When I was eleven, my friend Anjali and I disagreed about which team should go first in kabaddi. I shouted, “You're wrong!” and she stormed off. Our teacher took us both aside. She asked me, “Can you say it another way?” I said, “I see it differently. I think we should toss a coin, because that's fair.” Anjali stopped and thought. “I guess that's okay,” she said. I learned that saying “I see it differently, and here's why” is no rejection of the person. We played right after.

qa.q: What game were the friends arguing about?
qa.a: Kabaddi.

qa.q: What did the storyteller feel when Anjali stormed off?
qa.a: The storyteller was probably upset and surprised, since shouting “You're wrong!” had pushed the friend away.

qa.q: What could a child say instead of shouting in a disagreement?
qa.a: A child could say “I see it differently, and here's why,” as the storyteller learned to do.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt when she was shouted at compared with when the reason was given?
qa.a: She probably felt attacked when shouted at, and calmer and respected when a reason was offered.

grounding: A child learns to say I see it differently and give a reason, instead of shouting, so disagreement is not rejection of the person.

passage: The bus broke down on the way to the zoo trip, and the teacher went to phone the school. Gopika and Arnab, waiting by the roadside with their class, argued about whether to play word games or sing songs until help arrived. “Songs are boring!” said Arnab loudly. Gopika bit back what she wanted to say. Then she took a breath. “I see it differently. Songs help us all join in, and word games only work for some of us. What do you think?” Arnab folded his arms, then unfolded them. “Okay, maybe one of each,” he said. They started with a song.

qa.q: Where were the children waiting?
qa.a: By the roadside, after the bus broke down.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she bit back what she wanted to say, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at being called boring, but she took a breath and calmly explained her view.

qa.q: What did Gopika say that helped, compared with shouting or sulking?
qa.a: She said “I see it differently,” gave a reason and asked Arnab what he thought.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt when Gopika asked what he thought?
qa.a: He probably felt listened to, which may be why he unfolded his arms and offered a compromise.

grounding: A child says I see it differently and gives a reason and asks for the other view, so disagreement is not a rejection of the person.
